parts.visual:
A founder builds a company. It grows to $10 Million. Investors offer to invest $50 Million to make it a Billion-dollar company, but they demand the founder step down as CEO so they can hire a professional. Does the founder take the deal?

The Dilemma:
1. 'Rich': You give up control of your company (and your CEO title) to investors who can mathematically make you a billionaire.
2. 'King': You refuse all outside money so you can retain 100% control of your company forever, even if it means the company stays small.
parts.audio: The Founder's Dilemma forces every entrepreneur to make a brutal choice: Do you want to be 'Rich' or do you want to be 'King'? You rarely get to be both. You must choose between financial maximization and absolute control.

questions.question: A founder owns 100% of a company worth $1 Million. A VC offers to invest $10 Million, but the founder's ownership will drop to 40%. The founder rejects the deal because they 'refuse to let anyone tell them what to do'. What choice did they make?
options: They chose to be King. They prioritized absolute control over financial maximization. They would rather own 100% of a small pie than 40% of a massive pie.
questions.correct_answer: They chose to be King. They prioritized absolute control over financial maximization. They would rather own 100% of a small pie than 40% of a massive pie.
questions.explanation: There is no wrong answer, but you must know which path you are on from Day 1.

questions.question: Listen to the VC explaining why the founder must step down. What is the logic?
questions.tts_text: You are a brilliant engineer. You built an amazing prototype in your garage. But you have zero experience managing a 500-person global sales team. We need to hire a professional CEO to scale this.
options: The skills required to START a company are completely different from the skills required to SCALE a company. A self-aware founder (choosing 'Rich') steps aside when the company outgrows them.
The VC wants to be CEO.
questions.correct_answer: The skills required to START a company are completely different from the skills required to SCALE a company. A self-aware founder (choosing 'Rich') steps aside when the company outgrows them.
questions.explanation: Very few founders (like Mark Zuckerberg) possess the rare ability to transition from a garage hacker to a Fortune 500 CEO.

questions.question: Why do VCs almost always prefer a founder who wants to be 'Rich'?
options: Because a 'Rich' founder is willing to sell the company, step down, or take massive risks to achieve a billion-dollar valuation. A 'King' will sabotage the company to protect their own ego and CEO title.
questions.correct_answer: Because a 'Rich' founder is willing to sell the company, step down, or take massive risks to achieve a billion-dollar valuation. A 'King' will sabotage the company to protect their own ego and CEO title.
questions.explanation: If the founder's ego becomes larger than the company, the VC loses their investment.

questions.question: What is the psychological trap of the 'King' mentality?
options: They surround themselves with mediocre employees who will never challenge them (Yes Men). A 'King' is terrified of hiring executives smarter than themselves, leading to corporate stagnation.
questions.correct_answer: They surround themselves with mediocre employees who will never challenge them (Yes Men). A 'King' is terrified of hiring executives smarter than themselves, leading to corporate stagnation.
questions.explanation: A players hire A players. B players hire C players.
